'''Michelle Povinelli''' (born 1975) is a Professor of Electrical Engineering and Physics and Astronomy at the [[University of Southern California]] (USC) and Fellow of the [[The Optical Society|OSA]] and [[SPIE]]. Povinelli's research in nanophotonics focuses on the behavior of light inside complex materials.

Povinelli completed her doctoral research at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 2004, followed by a postdoc on [[Stanford University]] from 2004 to 2008. She became a professor at USC in 2008. In 2010, Povinelli was awarded a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers|Presidential Early Career Awards for Scientists and Engineers]]. She was appointed to a full professorship in 2018.

== Education and career ==
Povinelli received her bachelor's degree in physics from the [[University of Chicago]] and masters in physics from the [[University of Cambridge]], both in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://spie.org/x42604.xml?SSO=1 |title=Michelle Povinelli |work=Women in Optics |publisher=SPIE}}</ref> She completed a Ph.D. in physics titled ''Characteristics of defect modes, slow light, and disorder in photonic crystals'' at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 2004, with [[John Joannopoulos]] as her advisor.<ref>{{cite thesis |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/29449 |title=Characteristics of defect modes, slow light, and disorder in photonic crystals (Doctoral thesis) |first=Michelle Lynn |last=Povinelli |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |year=2004|hdl=1721.1/29449 |type=Thesis }}</ref> Povinelli was a postdoc at [[Stanford University|Stanford]] in the Gintzon Laboratory under a [[L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Awards|L'Oreal For Women in Science Postdoctoral Fellowship]] from 2004 to 2008.<ref name=":3">{{Cite magazine |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/84/i26/LOreal-USA-Honors-Women-Science.html |title=L'Oreal USA Honors Women In Science|date=June 26, 2006 |volume=84 |issue=26 |magazine=Chemical & Engineering News}}</ref> She joined the [[University of Southern California]] (USC) in 2008 under the Gabilan Assistant Professorship in the Women in Science and Engineering program.<ref name=":4">{{Cite press release |url=https://viterbi.usc.edu/news/news/2009/michelle-povinelli-doubles.htm|title=Double Distinction: Hsieh Department Assistant Professor Wins Two Prestigious Research Grants |publisher=USC Viterbi School of Engineering |date=September 27, 2009 |first=Eric |last=Mankin}}</ref>

Povinelli received two research awards in 2010: the [[National Science Foundation CAREER Awards|National Science Foundation Career Award]] and an [[United States Army Research Laboratory|Army Research Office]] Young Investigator Award.<ref name=":4" /> Povinelli became a Fellow of the [[The Optical Society|Optical Society of America]] in 2016 for contributions to the theory and application of light forces in optical nanostructures and for "the understanding and realization of nanostructures for solar energy conversion".<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |url=https://www.osa.org/en-us/awards_and_grants/fellow_members/recent_fellows/2017_fellows/ |title=2017 OSA Fellows |publisher=The Optical Society |year=2017}}</ref> In 2018, Povinelli was promoted to a full professorship at USC. That year, she and [[Lorraine Turcotte]] organised the Women in Science and Engineering Research Horizons Symposium following an anonymous donation of $20&nbsp;million towards increasing gender diversity in science at USC.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://viterbischool.usc.edu/news/2018/05/usc-women-in-science-and-engineering-wise-helps-junior-female-faculty-share-their-research/ |title=USC Women In Science and Engineering (WiSE) helps junior female faculty share their research |publisher=USC Viterbi School of Engineering |language=en-US |date=May 7, 2018 |first=Tilden |last=Chima}}</ref>

== Research ==
Povinelli's research is primarily in [[nanophotonics]], focusing on the behavior of light as it moves through devices like [[solar cell]]s and optical chips.

An early branch of research undertaken by Povinelli involved using [[laser]] beams to trap and assemble two-dimensional nano-structures - hundreds at a time - for creation of new materials and chemical filters. Unlike optical traps consisting of free-space laser beams, Povinelli patterned a [[Wafer (electronics)|silicon wafer]] with holes to create a [[photonic crystal]], each hole 300&nbsp;nm in diameter. Particles are then moved into the holes to form a square [[crystal lattice]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/91/web/2013/04/Building-New-Materials-Light.html|title=Building New Materials With Light {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|last=Katherine Bourzac|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=2019-08-16}}</ref>

Povinelli predicted and proved that light could exert a force when guided through silicon strip waveguides, which was shown to move a nearby strip. Such methods are useful for optical circuits and re-routing of signals. Another prediction of Povinelli is increased solar cell efficiency when incorporating nanostructures.<ref name=":0">{{Cite magazine |url=http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?TRID=965 |title=Innovator Under 35: Michelle Povinelli, 34 |magazine=MIT Technology Review |year=2010 |language=en-us}}</ref>

Working with [[Northrop Grumman]], Povinelli developed a new material able to self-regulate the temperature of satellites made of a mixture of silicon and [[Vanadium(IV) oxide|vanadium dioxide]]. To combat temperature variations of over 200 degrees Fahrenheit without relying on physical shutters or heat pipes that consume large amounts of power, the phase change behaviour of vanadium dioxide is used instead. At low temperatures it acts as an [[Insulator (electricity)|insulator]], and at high temperatures it is a [[Electrical conductor|conductor]] which radiates heat. With a 20 fold improvement in temperature management, this research may have applications in maintaining building temperatures.[https://doi.org/10.1364/OPTICA.4.001390]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/12/171213095558.htm|title=Thermal 'skin' designed to maintain temperature of satellites: VO2 coated silicon material performs 20 times better than current semiconductors|website=ScienceDaily|language=en|access-date=2019-08-16}}</ref>

In 2019 it was announced that the research group of Povinelli will work in the [[Breakthrough Starshot]] project, towards a proof-of-concept demonstration of ultra-fast light-driven nanocrafts. This is work towards the first launch to [[Alpha Centauri]], led by a consortium of scientists such as [[Steven Chu]], [[Mae Jemison]], and [[Martin Rees]]. Povinelli is working towards the [[Solar sail|light sail]] portion based on research on thermal regulation.[https://www.osapublishing.org/oe/abstract.cfm?uri=oe-27-15-21787]

== Personal life ==
Povinelli studies [[capoeira]]. In an interview with Viterabi Magazine, she describes capoeira as combining "hard physical training, elements of dance and music, and a strong sense of community".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://magazine.viterbi.usc.edu/spring-2015-2/changing-the-conversation/many-lives-of-engineers/|title=Many Lives of Engineers|website=USC Viterbi {{!}} Magazine|language=en-US|access-date=2019-08-16}}</ref>
